Physical Exam is a broad clinical procedure performed by healthcare providers to assess a patient's overall health status, detect signs of disease, and inform diagnosis and treatment decisions. It is a fundamental component of medical care, utilized in various contexts such as the diagnosis of basal cell skin cancer, testing for DCIS, determining the clinical stage before treatment, and serving as a surveillance method for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer. During oncology care, it is performed by an oncologist every 1 to 3 cycles of chemotherapy to monitor the patient's condition and is also used during surveillance to detect potential recurrence.

The examination typically involves checking vital signs, measuring height and weight, listening to the lungs and heart, and examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Providers also palpate body parts to assess organs and feel for enlarged lymph nodes, particularly in the neck, underarms, and groin. Depending on the clinical context, the exam may include specific assessments, such as a breast examination to check for abnormalities or palpation of the abdomen and pelvis to detect masses or other issues. It may also involve evaluating body systems and functional status to gauge physical ability.

As a general health check, the physical exam is a routine method for checking the body for signs of disease and assessing overall physical condition. It is a versatile tool used by various team members to evaluate a patient's health, detect abnormalities, and guide subsequent medical actions.

Medical History is a comprehensive record of a patient's past and current health information, encompassing all health issues, illnesses, injuries, symptoms, treatments, and medications a person has experienced throughout their life. This record serves as a foundational tool for healthcare providers, informing the care team about the patient's overall health status and guiding clinical decision-making. It is actively used to determine the best course of treatment for a patient, including in specific diagnostic contexts such as the evaluation of basal cell skin cancer. The information contained within a medical history is typically gathered during a medical consultation and may also include the health history of close blood relatives, providing a broader context for the patient's health. Ultimately, this detailed review of a patient's past and present health conditions is essential for informing medical decisions and ensuring appropriate, personalized care.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

The specific destinations for metastatic spread vary depending on the origin of the primary cancer. Common sites of secondary tumor formation include the lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and liver. For instance, metastasis from prostate cancer defines advanced-stage disease, while bladder cancer may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, or lungs. In the context of kidney cancer, metastasis refers to the formation of new tumors outside the kidney itself.

Clinically, the presence of metastasis often necessitates further diagnostic procedures, such as a biopsy, to confirm the spread and guide treatment decisions. The formation of these secondary tumors is a critical factor in cancer prognosis, as it indicates that the disease has become more complex and challenging to treat.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. Its health and function are commonly assessed through blood tests, such as a chemistry profile or liver function tests, and it can be imaged using MRI to detect signs of disease.

The liver is a frequent and clinically significant site for cancer metastasis. It is a common destination for cancer cells originating from various primary tumors, including breast, colon, rectal, anal, stomach, pancreatic, cervical, bladder, kidney, prostate, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancers. In many of these cases, such as with colon cancer, the liver is a primary site for stage 4 spread, while for others, like kidney cancer, it is a less frequent but still possible site of distant metastasis. The liver can also be affected by leukemia spreading outside the bloodstream, and cancer cell buildup in the organ can cause it to swell.

Beyond its role in metastasis, the liver is susceptible to damage from certain medical treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate. As an organ that processes chemicals, its function is critical to overall health, and its assessment is a standard part of medical diagnostics.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Surgery is a broad medical term for procedures that involve physical intervention, typically through an incision, to treat disease, remove cancer or other tissue, or repair the body. In oncology, it is a fundamental treatment modality used to physically remove tumors, cancerous tissue, and sometimes nearby lymph nodes. As a treatment for various cancers, its application and feasibility depend on the cancer type, stage, and location. For instance, it is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer and a primary treatment for early-stage cervical cancer, often involving the removal of cancerous tissue. For ovarian cancer, surgery is frequently the initial treatment, often performed by a gynecologic oncologist, and is typically followed by chemotherapy and maintenance therapy; its success depends on tumor size and location. In prostate cancer, surgery involves removing the cancerous tissue, which may include the tumor or the entire prostate, and is an option even for advanced stages. For bladder cancer, the procedure can range from removing the tumor to removing the entire bladder, depending on the stage, and may also involve removing surrounding tissue. In breast cancer, surgery is used as an initial treatment, after which pathologic staging provides more accurate details, and may involve the removal of breast tissue for analysis.

Surgery is also a key treatment for several other malignancies. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and for some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer to remove cancer from the body. For thyroid cancer, it is a standard treatment involving the physical removal of tissue, with targeted therapy used when surgery cannot be performed. It is a main treatment for glioma, involving tumor removal, and can be the sole treatment for grade 1 gliomas. For chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers, surgery is used to remove tumors. In anal cancer, surgery may be used to remove the anus if the disease does not respond to treatment or returns. However, surgery is not always possible or successful, such as for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and it is not normally an option for primary CNS lymphoma due to associated risks. Additionally, surgery may have increased side effects for smokers, and staging after the procedure provides more accurate details about the disease.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

About glioma What is a glioma? What causes a glioma? Are there types of gliomas? How are gliomas diagnosed? Can gliomas be cured? What’s next? Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Gliomas can be challenging to treat, but treatment is improving. What is a glioma? A glioma is a type of tumor that grows in the brain. A tumor is an abnormal growth of cells. Gliomas develop from certain brain cells called glial cells. Glial cells support the function of nerve cells (neurons) in the central nervous system (the brain and the spinal cord). Many types of tumors can occur in the central nervous system. Only those that start as glial cells become gliomas. Gliomas are the most common type of malignant (cancerous) brain tumor in adults. Gliomas can happen at any age but occur more often in adults than in children. Gliomas start in the brain or sometimes the spinal cord. But they rarely spread to another area of the body. What makes gliomas so complicated is that they invade and blend into the normal parts of the brain. So gliomas can be very difficult to treat without harming the healthy parts of the brain. Normal cells vs. cancer cells Normal cells follow the body’s rules. Normal cells increase in number only when they’re needed, and they die when they’re old or damaged. Cancer cells don’t follow the rules. Cancer cells can multiply quickly and avoid dying. Cancer cells can crowd out normal cells and take their place. Eventually this damages the body and often results in symptoms. What causes a glioma? No one knows exactly what causes most brain tumors, including gliomas. What experts do know is that brain tumors often start with an abnormality (mutation) in certain cells. This abnormality causes these cells to grow out of control (become cancerous). This type of mutation happens on its own. It’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Gliomas occur in both children and adults. This book discusses gliomas only in adults. Are there types of gliomas? There are several types of glioma tumors. The 3 most common types are astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas. They’re made of different kinds of glial cells. Astrocytomas look like star-shaped glial cells called astrocytes. The main job of astrocytes is to maintain the chemical environment that allows communication between nerve cells. Oligodendrogliomas look like oligodendrocytes, which are glial cells that protect electrical signaling in nerve cells. Glioblastomas come from precursor cells that develop into cells like astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. Glioblastomas are the most destructive and dangerous type of glioma tumor. Besides tumor type, gliomas are also categorized by grade. The grade indicates how fast the tumor is likely to grow. A low-grade glioma usually grows slowly while a high-grade glioma often grows rapidly. Although it helps to put gliomas into categories, it’s important to note that each glioma has its own molecular characteristics and behavior. That also means that each person’s glioma is unique. So your progress and experience will be unique to you. Gliomas often occur in the upper part of the brain where they can disrupt important brain functions. Few gliomas in adults have distinct and welldefined edges like the one in this illustration. Most gliomas blend deeply into normal brain tissue and have vague borders. This makes them very difficult to remove entirely. When the tumor is removed, some tumor cells must be left behind to avoid damaging nearby brain tissue. How are gliomas diagnosed? A glioma is often found when it starts causing symptoms. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may be a sign of disease. Gliomas cause symptoms when they put pressure on the brain or invade brain tissue. Some people have many symptoms while others don’t have any. Common symptoms of gliomas include: Unusual or frequent headaches Seizures Changes in personality or mood Nausea and vomiting Difficulty speaking or swallowing Muscle weakness Difficulty with walking, balance, or coordination Symptoms provide clues that something is wrong. But they don’t provide enough information to identify a specific illness. Different tests, physical exams, and surgical procedures are required to diagnose a glioma. If these tests show that you have a glioma, your care team will discuss your treatment options with you. If possible, seek care at a center with experience in treating brain tumors. Diagnosis vs. prognosis What’s the difference between your diagnosis and your prognosis? These two words sound alike but they’re very different. Diagnosis: The identification of an illness based on tests. The diagnosis names what illness you have. Prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease. The prognosis predicts how your disease will turn out. Can gliomas be cured? Most gliomas are not curable, but they are usually treatable. Treatment can slow down the tumor’s growth for a period of time, reduce its symptoms, and prolong life. The main treatments for a glioma are surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. These are often combined with one another for more complete treatment. Another option to consider is participating in a clinical trial for a potential new treatment. Treatment may be able to stop the glioma from growing and keep it stabilized for a time. This may last for months or years. However, even with the best treatment, gliomas usually grow back eventually. So periodic follow-up visits and additional rounds of treatment are recommended. It’s

Treatment Plan is a comprehensive, personalized strategy for treating cancer, developed by a multidisciplinary care team in collaboration with the patient. It is primarily determined by diagnostic results, including imaging studies, biopsies, and blood tests, which help establish the cancer's stage and grade. The plan is designed to guide the selection of the most appropriate therapy, taking into account critical factors such as the patient's performance status and personal preferences. It may be tailored for specific conditions, such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where the approach is chosen jointly by the patient and care team based on test outcomes. The plan can be highly specific, detailing elements like radiation doses and the number of treatment sessions, or it can be a broader proposed course of medical treatment. Ultimately, the Treatment Plan is a documented agreement that outlines the agreed-upon cancer treatment, potential side effects, therapeutic goals, and other essential care details, ensuring all parties are aligned on the path forward.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Fertility is the ability to conceive or have children, a consideration that applies to individuals of all genders. In the context of cancer care, fertility is a significant health concern because cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and other modalities—can adversely affect a person’s reproductive capacity. This impact is relevant across various cancer types, such as follicular lymphoma, head and neck cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and anal cancer, among others.

Such discussions allow for proactive measures, including fertility testing for all genders, to assess and preserve reproductive potential. The upper part of the vagina and pelvic lymph nodes may also be removed. Trachelectomy is a fertility-sparing surgery. The uterus and ovaries are left intact, allowing for the possibility of natural pregnancy in the future. In a simple trachelectomy, only the cervix is removed. An extrafascial (simple) hysterectomy removes only the uterus (including the cervix). Extrafascial hysterectomy can be performed through the vagina, through the abdomen, or using a minimally invasive approach. This type is most commonly used for stage IA1 cancer. A modified radical hysterectomy removes the uterus (including the cervix), a portion of the connective tissue that holds the cervix in place, and about a half inch or less of the vagina. Modified radical hysterectomy is performed through the abdomen. A radical hysterectomy removes the uterus (including the cervix), much of the connective tissue that holds the cervix in place, and the top quarter or third of the vagina. There are shortand long-term symptoms and risks of surgical menopause that can greatly affect quality of life. When caused by surgery, the symptoms of menopause may be sudden and more severe. Symptoms include hot flashes, sleeping problems, night sweats, weight gain, and changes in mood. Vaginal atrophy is another common symptom. Vaginal atrophy is a condition in which the lining of the vagina becomes thin, dry, and inflamed. Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Lynch Syndrome is a hereditary condition caused by mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, which leads to a deficiency in DNA repair mechanisms. This inherited syndrome is the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine (endometrial) cancers, and it significantly increases the risk of developing colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Beyond these primary sites, Lynch Syndrome is also associated with an elevated risk for other malignancies, including pancreatic cancer, adrenal tumors, and cancers of the urinary tract, such as bladder cancer. The condition is recognized as a key factor in clinical decision-making, particularly when considering germline testing for individuals with a personal or family history suggestive of these cancers. As an inherited cancer syndrome, Lynch Syndrome is fundamentally linked to an increased susceptibility to a broad spectrum of cancers, with colon and uterine cancers being the most prominent, followed by ovarian and other extracolonic malignancies.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

Colon cancer is a disease characterized by the growth of malignant cells in the colon, a part of the large intestine. It is a distinct form of cancer with treatment approaches that differ from those used for rectal cancer. The disease commonly originates from polyps, particularly adenomatous polyps, which are abnormal growths on the inner lining of the colon that can become cancerous over time. Colon cancer is considered a common and treatable form of cancer, especially when detected early, and it can present in various stages, including stages 1, 2, and 3, as well as in non-metastatic or metastatic forms.

The condition may be linked to family history, suggesting a potential genetic or hereditary component that can increase an individual's risk. Additionally, research indicates that having colon cancer may be associated with an elevated risk of developing prostate cancer. As a disease, colon cancer involves the uncontrolled division of abnormal cells within the colon, and its progression and severity are typically classified by staging systems that help guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

What is primary CNS lymphoma? What causes primary CNS lymphoma? How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Can primary CNS lymphoma be cured? What’s next? Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make wellinformed decisions. What is primary CNS lymphoma? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). But people with primary CNS lymphoma often have one or more of these risk factors: Having an immunodeficiency disorder, which is an illness that weakens the immune system’s ability to fight infections and diseases. Primary CNS lymphoma is frequently linked to HIV, the immunodeficiency virus that causes AIDS. Carrying the Epstein-Barr virus, which is the virus that causes mononucleosis (“mono”) and other illnesses. Epstein-Barr is one of the most common viruses in humans. Most people are infected with it. After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Having an autoimmune disease, such as lupus, in which the immune system overreacts and attacks healthy tissues and organs. Having an organ transplant, which requires medications that suppress the immune system. This leads to a higher risk of infections. Being an older adult. Although primary CNS lymphoma can occur at any age, the majority of people diagnosed with it are in their 60s or 70s. How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Other such symptoms may include changes in personality or behavior, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control (incontinence), or difficulty speaking or swallowing. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Bladder cancer basics About bladder cancer Bladder cancer treatment Key points Having cancer can be worrisome and stressful. This book will help you understand your diagnosis of bladder cancer. It will also explain your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make well-informed decisions about what’s best for you. This may reduce some of the fear and worry. About bladder cancer What is bladder cancer? Bladder cancer is a disease that occurs when cells in the inner lining of the bladder grow out of control. The bladder is a hollow, balloonlike organ that stores urine. It’s located in your pelvis—the area between your hip bones in your lower abdomen. The bladder’s inner lining, called the urothelium, prevents urine from leaking back into the body. What does the bladder do? • The bladder is a hollow organ in the lower pelvis. Its main job is to store urine (pee). In adults, the bladder can hold up to 2 cups of urine. • Urine is made by the kidneys and flows down to the bladder through two tubes called ureters. • The bladder gets bigger as it fills with urine and gets smaller when you pee. It’s about the size of an orange when empty and the size of a grapefruit when full. When you urinate, the muscles in the walls of the bladder contract. This forces the urine out of the bladder and through a tube called the urethra, which streams it out of the body. • Together, these organs are called the urinary tract. Bladder cancer happens when abnormal (cancer) cells develop genetic errors (mutations) that cause them to make many more cancer cells. Cancer cells also avoid normal cell death. As cancer cells increase, they crowd out and overwhelm normal cells. Over time, the cancer cells may form a tumor in the bladder. Sometimes the cells grow deeper and invade the bladder’s muscle layer. The cancer may even break through the bladder and spread to other parts of the body. Is bladder cancer common? Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers in adults. Most people who have bladder cancer are aged 55 years and over. Bladder cancer is often found at an early stage when the cancer is highly treatable. However, bladder cancer commonly comes back again even after treatment. In many cases, bladder cancer comes back in a different place and sometimes more advanced than before. That’s why follow-up testing is so important. People with bladder cancer need regular follow-up tests for many years to check if the cancer has returned. The most common kind of bladder cancer starts in the urothelial cells, which are stretchy cells that line the inside of the bladder. Urothelial cells also form the inner layer in the rest of the urinary tract, which includes the kidneys, the ureters, and the urethra. Cancer of the urothelium can start in these areas instead of the bladder, although it’s less common. Other (non-urothelial) types of bladder cancer are much less common. Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Smoking is the act of inhaling and exhaling smoke from tobacco products, and it is a major behavioral risk factor for numerous cancers and other diseases. Objectively, smoking is identified as the main cause of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer, accounting for about half of all cases. It also increases the risks of developing and dying from prostate cancer, and is a significant risk factor for cervical cancer, anal cancer, and cancers of the head and neck, lung, and other sites.

Beyond increasing cancer incidence, smoking adversely affects cancer treatment. It can limit the effectiveness of therapies, increase treatment-related side effects and toxicity, and impair wound healing. Consequently, smoking is a habit that negatively impacts overall treatment outcomes. Conversely, quitting smoking can lead to better cancer treatment results and reduced health risks. As a health-related behavior, smoking is generally advised to be quit, with counseling support recommended to assist individuals in overcoming the habit.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Doctor is a medical professional who provides comprehensive patient care, including performing diagnostic procedures such as biopsies, digital rectal exams, and laryngoscopy, as well as interpreting their results. This physician advises on treatment options, including birth control choices, and considers risk factors for conditions like cervical cancer. The doctor orders imaging tests, discusses fertility risks, and informs patients about treatment plans, while also receiving and reviewing reports from radiologists to oversee patient care and discuss findings with the patient. Additionally, the doctor recommends diagnostic tests for conditions such as bladder cancer, may suggest genetic testing, and provides guidance on lifestyle factors like exercise, diet, aspirin use, and smoking cessation, alongside cancer treatment decisions. For specialized cases, this medical professional should have experience in diagnosing and treating specific types of bone cancer.

Physical Exam is a broad clinical procedure performed by healthcare providers to assess a patient's overall health status, detect signs of disease, and inform diagnosis and treatment decisions. It is a fundamental component of medical care, utilized in various contexts such as the diagnosis of basal cell skin cancer, testing for DCIS, determining the clinical stage before treatment, and serving as a surveillance method for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer. During oncology care, it is performed by an oncologist every 1 to 3 cycles of chemotherapy to monitor the patient's condition and is also used during surveillance to detect potential recurrence.

The examination typically involves checking vital signs, measuring height and weight, listening to the lungs and heart, and examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Providers also palpate body parts to assess organs and feel for enlarged lymph nodes, particularly in the neck, underarms, and groin. Depending on the clinical context, the exam may include specific assessments, such as a breast examination to check for abnormalities or palpation of the abdomen and pelvis to detect masses or other issues. It may also involve evaluating body systems and functional status to gauge physical ability.

As a general health check, the physical exam is a routine method for checking the body for signs of disease and assessing overall physical condition. It is a versatile tool used by various team members to evaluate a patient's health, detect abnormalities, and guide subsequent medical actions.

Treatment for more advanced stage (muscle-invasive) bladder cancer can be complicated but it may still get rid of the cancer. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment provides a longer and more comfortable life with fewer symptoms. It’s important to know that bladder cancer commonly comes back even after treatment. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy (nasolaryngoscopy) uses a small flexible scope passed through your nose and into your throat. Numbing medicine will be sprayed in your nose. Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.

The two main hormones made by the thyroid are thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). People who are younger, healthier, and more physically fit have a better chance for a cure. In most people, primary CNS lymphoma can’t be cured, but it can be treated. Treatment can slow down its growth and reduce its symptoms for a period of time, and prolong life. The main treatments for primary CNS lymphoma include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplant, or a combination of these treatments. Joining a clinical trial of a potential new therapy is another recommended option. Treatment may be able to put primary CNS lymphoma into remission. Remission means there are no symptoms or signs of cancer. Remission may last for months or years. However, even with the best treatment, primary CNS lymphoma often comes back (relapses) in the brain, spinal cord, or the eye. It’s true that primary CNS lymphoma is fatal for some patients. In the past few years, improved detection methods have shortened the time to diagnosis and led to better outcomes, even in people with weakened immune systems. Medicines are available during treatment to help reduce most of these side effects. Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Treatment Plan is a comprehensive, personalized strategy for treating cancer, developed by a multidisciplinary care team in collaboration with the patient. It is primarily determined by diagnostic results, including imaging studies, biopsies, and blood tests, which help establish the cancer's stage and grade. The plan is designed to guide the selection of the most appropriate therapy, taking into account critical factors such as the patient's performance status and personal preferences. It may be tailored for specific conditions, such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where the approach is chosen jointly by the patient and care team based on test outcomes. The plan can be highly specific, detailing elements like radiation doses and the number of treatment sessions, or it can be a broader proposed course of medical treatment. Ultimately, the Treatment Plan is a documented agreement that outlines the agreed-upon cancer treatment, potential side effects, therapeutic goals, and other essential care details, ensuring all parties are aligned on the path forward.

Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.

The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. Often, in CML the very immature or most immature cells (myeloblasts or lymphoblasts) are referred to simply as blasts. CML is thought to arise from blood stem cells that make an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells. However, an advanced form of CML, called blast phase CML (BP-CML), can cause an increased amount of lymphoid or myeloid progenitor cells. The type of blast phase cell will affect treatment in BP-CML. What causes CML? The cause of CML can be traced to a single, specific abnormal gene called BCR::ABLThis fused gene occurs when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and switch places. This creates a new, abnormal chromosome 22 that contains a small part of chromosome This new chromosome is referred to as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph) and is the hallmark of CML. If you do not have the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene, you do not have CML. BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells. It is not passed down from birth parents to children. The BCR::ABL1 gene makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth. This growth ultimately leads to CML. Treatment for CML aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. Those with CML should be treated at centers experienced in this type of cancer. What can you do to get the best care? Advocate for yourself. You have an important role to play in your care. In fact, you’re more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with your care team. Consider seeking the opinion of a CML specialist. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients will help you understand cancer care. With better understanding, you’ll be more prepared to discuss your care with your team and share your concerns. Lung cancer basics What is NSCLC? What is early and locally advanced NSCLC? What’s the best treatment? Key points If you’re reading this, you or someone you care for might have non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It’s the most common type of lung cancer. In this chapter, you’ll learn what this type of cancer is and what it means if it’s early or locally advanced. What is NSCLC? Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a type of lung cancer. Another type of lung cancer is small cell lung cancer, but it is a different cancer covered in another book. Lung cancer cells grow out of control. They don’t die when they should and make many new cancer cells, which become tumors. Lung cancer cells also don’t stay in place. They can break away from a tumor, spread outside the lung, and form more tumors. NSCLC is a type of lung carcinoma Almost all lung cancers are carcinomas (karsin-OH-mas). Lung carcinomas form from cells that line the airways of the lungs. The airways inside the lungs are the bronchi, bronchioli, and alveoli. NSCLC is the most common lung carcinoma. Other lung carcinomas are neuroendocrine tumors. Information on lung neuroendocrine tumors can be found at Airways of the lungs The air you breathe moves through a series of airways. It travels down your throat and through your windpipe (trachea). The windpipe splits into two airways called bronchi. Inside the lung, each bronchus divides into smaller airways called the bronchioli. At the end of the bronchioli are sacs called alveoli. Oxygen is transferred from air into the blood in the alveoli. NSCLC, found at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. What are the causes and risk factors? Smoking cigarettes is the main cause of SCLC. Almost everyone with SCLC smokes or has smoked. Many people with SCLC have regularly smoked more than a pack a day. Exposure to second-hand smoke also increases the risk of lung cancer. Secondhand smoke is the smoke exhaled by another person and the smoke from combustible tobacco products. Although rare in Western countries, there are occasions where people with no smoking history develop this disease. There are other unknown causes of SCLC. Researchers are still learning why some people who smoke never get lung cancer and others who have never smoked do. A person’s chances of getting SCLC are higher in the following situations: Over 70 years of age Prior radiation therapy to the chest Exposure to cancer-causing chemicals (also known as carcinogens), such as radon and asbestos If you don’t smoke, don’t start. If you do smoke, quit. New lung tumors are less likely to develop after quitting smoking. Nicotine addiction is one of the hardest addictions to stop. The stress of having cancer may make it even harder to quit. There is help. Ask your health care providers about counseling and medicines to help you quit. What are the symptoms of SCLC? SCLC can cause many types of symptoms. The symptoms depend on where the lung tumor has grown to or spread. SCLC can prevent the lungs from getting the air they need. Some people also have symptoms from paraneoplastic syndromes, which are caused by an abnormal body response to lung cancer. Some symptoms caused by SCLC are listed in Guide SCLC is often found when it’s causing symptoms or routine blood tests are abnormal. Less often, it’s found in x-rays or CT scans before symptoms start. Unlike other lung cancers, it’s difficult to detect SCLC early because it grows more quickly. Airways of the lungs Air moves through your body in a series of airways. It travels down your throat and through the windpipe (trachea). The windpipe splits into 2 airways called bronchi. Inside the lung, each bronchus branches off into the parts of the lung, called lobes. The right lung has 3 lobes, and the left lung has 2 lobes. The bronchi divide into smaller airways called the bronchioli. At the end of the bronchioli are sacs called alveoli. Oxygen is transferred from air into the blood in the alveoli. Your primary care provider may be the first to suspect that you have lung cancer. You will need to see specialists to determine if you have cancer. Your assessment team may include the following board-certified experts: Thoracic radiologist Interventional radiologist Pulmonologist Thoracic surgeon Medical oncologist Radiation oncologist To confirm that you have cancer, you’ll need testing of your body tissue or fluid. Small samples will be removed from your body during a procedure called a biopsy.
The esophagus Parts of the esophagus Esophageal cancer How cancer spreads Key points The esophagus is a long, muscular tube through which food passes from the throat to the stomach. Esophageal cancer starts when abnormal cells grow out of control in the layers of the esophagus inner lining. The esophagus The esophagus is located behind the trachea (windpipe) and in front of the spine. It is part of the digestive system. The digestive system transports and breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, and removes waste from the body. It includes the esophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine, colon, rectum, and anus. Food and drink enter the mouth and move through the esophagus into the stomach. When you swallow, small contractions, called peristalsis, along with gravity and pressure, move food down the esophagus and into the stomach. Except during the act of swallowing, the esophagus is normally empty. The esophagus is about 10 inches long and about 1 inch wide. It has two sphincters, circular muscles that normally remain closed except during the act of swallowing. One sphincter is located at the top of the esophagus and the other at the bottom, between the esophagus and the stomach. The digestive tract The digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract is part of the digestive system. Food enters the mouth and passes through the esophagus into the stomach. After being broken down into a liquid, food enters the small intestine. The large intestine prepares unused food to be moved out of the body. Parts of the esophagus Esophagus wall The esophagus wall contains 4 layers: Mucosa – inner membrane that is in contact with food. It has 3 parts: Epithelium – innermost lining and is normally made up of flat, thin cells called squamous cells Lamina propria – thin layer of connective tissue under the epithelium Muscularis mucosa - very thin layer of muscle under the lamina propria Submucosa – layer of connective tissue just below the mucosa that contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels. In some parts of the esophagus, this layer also includes glands that secrete mucus. Muscularis propria – thick layer of muscle under the submucosa. It contracts in a coordinated way to push food down the esophagus from the throat to the stomach (peristalsis). Tunica adventitia – outermost layer, made of connective tissue Upper esophagus The upper part of the esophagus is made of striated muscle. Striated muscle generates force and contracts. It is under your control (voluntary). Middle esophagus The middle part of the esophagus is a mixture of striated and smooth muscle. Lower esophagus The lower part of the esophagus consists only of smooth muscle. Smooth muscle is not under your control. It is
